description: "An open graduate textbook that connects modern machine learning to forecasting, financial econometrics, dependent data, and predictive-distribution evaluation."

# MLmetrics: Machine Learning for Econometricians {.unnumbered}

This open textbook introduces modern machine-learning (ML) methods for graduate students in econometrics. The aim is not to replace econometric reasoning with black-box prediction, but to show how flexible ML tools can be used carefully in the settings econometricians face in practice: forecasting, financial risk, macroeconomic data, or firm-level panels.

The book assumes a strong background in econometrics and statistics, but no prior exposure to machine learning. Each method is introduced from first principles and connected to familiar econometric ideas such as likelihood, forecast evaluation, time-series dependence, and model selection.

## Why Does This Book Exist? {.unnumbered}

This book grew out of two related motivations. The first was curiosity about how modern machine-learning methods should be adapted to the econometric problems that arise in research on forecasting, macro-finance, and predictive distributions. The second was teaching the master's-level course Machine Learning in Econometrics at the Econometrics Institute at Erasmus University Rotterdam.

In that course, I kept running into the same problem: standard ML texts are usually written for a different audience. They often assume little prior statistical training, work mostly with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data, and motivate ideas with image or text classification. The econometric issues that arise naturally in economic and financial applications — serial dependence, distributional forecasting, real-time information sets, and leakage from invalid validation designs — usually receive much less attention. At the same time, econometrics texts that discuss prediction or regularization rarely connect those topics to the broader ML toolkit, and seldom explain how methods such as neural networks or gradient boosting should be adapted when the data have the structure of a macroeconomic or financial time series.

The aim of these notes is to fill that gap directly. They are not a substitute for the many strong ML resources that already exist. Instead, they frame modern machine learning in a language that econometricians recognize, with the guiding question: how can we use flexible methods while respecting the information sets, dependence structures, and evaluation problems that arise in econometric work?

:::{.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Who This Book Is For

This book is written for students in econometrics, economics, finance, and related quantitative fields.

Readers should be comfortable with probability, mathematical statistics, regression, likelihood-based estimation, and basic time-series methods. No prior knowledge of neural networks, random forests, boosting, or conformal prediction is assumed. 
:::

## What You Will Learn {.unnumbered}

Machine-learning examples are often presented in clean i.i.d. settings. Econometric applications rarely look like that. Across the book, the emphasis is on the parts of machine learning that matter when that assumption breaks down:

- evaluating predictions when dependence, nonstationarity, and information sets matter
- using flexible models without contaminating estimated out-of-sample performance through leakage or invalid validation designs
- thinking about predictive distributions, scoring rules, tail risk, and uncertainty quantification
- the behavior of neural networks and tree-based methods in economic and financial applications
- tuning, comparing, and diagnosing models in a way that remains statistically defensible

## Book Roadmap {.unnumbered}

The book contains fifteen teaching chapters organized into four parts, followed by a reference appendix for the datasets used in the empirical examples.

| Part | Chapters | Focus |
|------|----------|-------|
| Background | [Information Theory](information_theory.qmd), [Cross Validation](cross_validation.qmd), [Evaluating Predictive Distributions](evaluating_distributions.qmd), [Optimization](optimization.qmd) | Core tools for measuring uncertainty, selecting models, evaluating forecasts, and training flexible models. |
| Neural Networks | [Feed-Forward Networks](feed_forward_nns.qmd), [Recurrent Networks](recurrent_neural_networks.qmd), [Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Networks](lstm_neural_networks.qmd), [Empirical Illustration: Realized Volatility](nn_example.qmd), [Distribution Modeling](distributions_via_nns.qmd) | Neural-network models for nonlinear prediction, sequential data, and distributional forecasting. |
| Tree-Based Methods | [Decision Trees](decision_trees.qmd), [Random Forests](random_forests.qmd), [Gradient Boosting](gradient_boosting.qmd), [Advanced Tree-Based Methods](adv_tree_based_methods.qmd) | Interpretable trees, variance reduction by forests, stagewise boosting, and distributional tree methods. |
| Further Topics | [Advanced Hyperparameter Optimization](hpo.qmd), [Conformal Prediction](conformal_prediction.qmd) | Modern tools for tuning and uncertainty quantification. |
| Reference Appendix | [Data Sets Used in This Book](datasets.qmd) | Sources, variables, and loading instructions for the file-backed datasets used in the empirical examples. |

## How To Use This Book {.unnumbered}

Each chapter combines formal notation, econometric interpretation, and Python examples. The code chunks are there to make the ideas concrete, but the mathematical arguments are written so the central logic can be followed without running code.

The exercises in the methods chapters are designed with handwritten exam preparation in mind. They emphasize derivations, forecast-evaluation logic, validation pitfalls, and conceptual distinctions that matter when machine-learning methods are applied to economic data.

## Why Python? {.unnumbered}

Many econometricians work primarily in R, and R has excellent support for statistical modeling and time-series analysis. This book uses Python because the modern ML ecosystem — including Keras with its TensorFlow backend, scikit-learn, and Optuna, the tools used here — is centered there, and students who go on to work with deep learning or foundation models will encounter Python as the default. The focus throughout remains on model choice, loss functions, validation design, and forecast evaluation rather than on software for its own sake.

## What This Book Does Not Cover {.unnumbered}

This book is not a general introduction to econometrics, and it is not a full treatment of time-series econometrics. It does not replace a dedicated treatment of autoregressive integrated moving-average (ARIMA) models, generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (GARCH) models, state-space models, causal inference, or asymptotic theory. Those topics are assumed as background when needed.

It is also not a software-engineering manual. The code examples are there to make the statistical ideas concrete, not to provide production-ready ML pipelines.

## How This Book Relates to Other Resources {.unnumbered}

Several good resources cover adjacent territory, and it helps to say briefly how this book fits in. The list below is not exhaustive; it names the resources closest in spirit to this book.

@CoqueretGuida2020 provide a practitioner-oriented guide to ML in asset pricing, with a focus on return prediction and portfolio formation. This book covers less on portfolio construction but more on time-series validation, distributional scoring rules, conformal prediction under dependence, and the econometric interpretation of neural-network and tree methods.

Standard ML textbooks such as @JamesWittenHastieTibshirani2013 are excellent starting points. This book complements them by assuming readers already understand regression and likelihood and concentrating on how ML methods should be adapted to non-i.i.d. econometric settings.

For readers who want a comprehensive, probability-first treatment of machine learning itself, the two volumes by Kevin Murphy [@Murphy2022PML1; @Murphy2023PML2] are the natural reference. They develop the full statistical machinery behind modern ML in far greater breadth than this book attempts; this book instead selects the methods most relevant to econometric forecasting problems and works out their behavior under dependence, heteroskedasticity, and real-time information constraints.
